solution.concept_anchor: Article 268 — levy vs. appropriation distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students familiar with Finance Commission tax-sharing instinctively assume Union-levied taxes are always shared, not fully retained by States.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Article 268 duties are not shared between Union and States — States retain 100% collected within their territory.
Eliminate (c): These duties are levied by the Union, not by States independently — States only collect and appropriate them.
Eliminate (d): Stamp duties under Article 268 are not part of the divisible pool — they are outside the Finance Commission sharing framework entirely.
Confirm (b): Article 268 duties are levied by Union, collected and appropriated fully by States — no sharing with Union.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often assume all Union-levied taxes involve some form of sharing with the Centre, given the prominence of the divisible pool concept. Article 268 is a deliberate exception — States retain every rupee collected within their territory from stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, and promissory notes. The trap worsens because Article 268 duties look identical to shared taxes at first glance (Union levies them), yet the appropriation is 100% State-level. Confusing this with Article 270 (divisible pool) or Article 269 (assigned taxes) is the most common error.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 268 of the Constitution creates a category where the Union government levies certain duties, but both collection and appropriation are handled entirely by the States. Currently this covers stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, bills of lading, letters of credit, and similar instruments.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: These duties are not shared between Union and States. States keep 100% of what is collected within their territory — the Union receives nothing.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Union levies the duty but States collect and appropriate the entire proceeds — this is the defining feature of Article 268.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: States do not levy these duties; levy power rests with Union alone. States exercise only collection and appropriation rights.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 268 duties are completely outside the divisible pool; Finance Commission has no role in distributing them.

Value Addition:
• Post-101st Amendment, medicinal and toilet preparations (formerly under Article 268) were subsumed under GST, narrowing the scope of this article.
• Article 268 ≠ Article 269: Under 269, taxes are 'assigned' to States; under 268, States 'collect and appropriate' — both result in States keeping 100%, but the constitutional terminology differs.
• This article reflects a federalism principle: revenue from transactions primarily local in character should accrue to the State where the transaction occurs.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 268-A vs. Article 269-A — constitutional numbering trap

statement_analysis.statement: Article 268-A, which dealt with service tax sharing, was inserted by the 88th Constitutional Amendment and was later repealed by the 101st Constitutional Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The 88th Amendment (2003) inserted Article 268-A to operationalize service tax sharing; it was specifically repealed by the 101st Amendment (2016) when GST subsumed service tax.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 269-A, inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment, provides that GST on inter-State supplies shall be levied and collected by the Union and the proceeds shall be apportioned entirely to the States.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 269-A, IGST proceeds are apportioned between the Union and the States — not entirely to States. Parliament prescribes the apportionment formula on the GST Council's recommendation.

statement_analysis.statement: The GST Council is empowered under Article 269-A to recommend the formula for apportioning IGST between the Union and States.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 269-A(2) mandates that the apportionment of IGST be made on Parliament's law based on GST Council recommendations — the Council recommends, Parliament enacts.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three feels correct because statements 1 and 3 are accurate, and Statement 2's error (regarding 'entirely to States') is subtle enough to escape detection under time pressure.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: 88th Amendment inserted Art. 268-A; 101st Amendment repealed it — both facts confirmed. Statement 1 is Correct.
Scrutinize Statement 2: IGST under Art. 269-A is apportioned between Union AND States — not entirely to States. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: GST Council recommends apportionment formula under Art. 269-A — confirmed. Statement 3 is Correct.
Correct statements are 1 and 3 only — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The numbering proximity of Article 268-A and 269-A is a classic UPSC trap. Article 268-A (now repealed) dealt with service tax; Article 269-A deals with IGST on inter-State supplies. Candidates who mix these up will misattribute provisions. Additionally, Statement 2 exploits a scope-extension error — students know IGST goes to States but forget the Union also retains a share, making 'entirely to States' sound plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
The 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) was transformative — it repealed Article 268-A (service tax sharing, inserted by the 88th Amendment in 2003) and inserted Articles 269-A and 279-A to accommodate GST.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 268-A's lifecycle is precisely 88th Amendment (insertion) → 101st Amendment (repeal). This is a frequently tested constitutional evolution fact.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: IGST proceeds under Article 269-A are shared between the Union and States — not given entirely to States. The Union retains its share of IGST as well. This is fundamentally different from Article 269 where proceeds are 'assigned' 100% to States.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 269-A(2) explicitly requires Parliament to formulate apportionment on the basis of GST Council recommendations — establishing a consultative constitutional mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Import transactions are treated as inter-State supply under Article 269-A — IGST on imports is thus shared, while customs duty remains solely with the Union.
• Article 269-A was a constitutional innovation: no prior article had created a shared-levy mechanism for a specific transaction type outside the Finance Commission framework.
• IGST revenue is NOT part of the divisible pool — it operates under a separate apportionment mechanism, making it distinct from Article 270 taxes.

solution.concept_anchor: Surcharges and cesses excluded from divisible pool — Article 271

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 271, Parliament may impose surcharges on taxes in the Union List, and the proceeds must be distributed among States through the Finance Commission formula.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 271 explicitly states that proceeds of surcharges go solely to the Union — they are excluded from the divisible pool and States receive nothing from surcharges.

statement_analysis.statement: Cesses such as the Health and Education Cess and the Swachh Bharat Cess form part of the divisible pool and are therefore subject to Finance Commission–recommended devolution.
statement_analysis.reason: Cesses, like surcharges, are excluded from the divisible pool under the constitutional framework — States receive no share of cess proceeds, which is a major fiscal federalism concern.

statement_analysis.statement: The growing proportion of cesses and surcharges in the Union's gross tax revenue effectively reduces the size of the divisible pool available for State devolution.
statement_analysis.reason: Since cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, any increase in their share in total tax collection directly shrinks the pool States benefit from — this is precisely the concern raised by the 15th Finance Commission.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Selecting only Statement 1 as incorrect seems tempting because the surcharge exclusion is a well-known fact, but Statement 2's error about cesses is equally important and equally incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Surcharge proceeds under Art. 271 go solely to Union — the claim that they are distributed via Finance Commission is wrong. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Cesses are also excluded from the divisible pool — stating they are 'subject to Finance Commission devolution' is wrong. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Growing cesses/surcharges do shrink the divisible pool — this is factually accurate and a recognized fiscal federalism concern. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements NOT correct are 1 and 2 only — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The cess trap is particularly potent: many students know surcharges go to the Union but assume cesses, because they are purpose-specific (Health, Education, Swachh Bharat), might be shared with States. In reality, both surcharges and cesses are outside the divisible pool. This is one of the most significant contemporary fiscal federalism controversies because the Union has progressively expanded cess collection, shrinking what States can claim through Finance Commission devolution.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 271 empowers Parliament to levy surcharges on any Union List tax, with proceeds reserved exclusively for the Union. Cesses operate under a similar constitutional logic — both are excluded from the divisible pool under Article 270's framework.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Surcharge proceeds go solely to the Union, not to States. Finance Commission has no authority over surcharge distribution.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Cesses are equally excluded. Despite being purpose-labelled (Health and Education Cess, Swachh Bharat Cess), States receive no share — making this a live fiscal federalism controversy.
• Statement 3 — Correct: As the Union raises more revenue through cesses and surcharges (which grew from ~4% to over 15% of gross tax revenue over two decades), the divisible pool proportionally shrinks — reducing absolute devolution to States even when percentage devolution remains constant.

Value Addition:
• The 15th Finance Commission explicitly flagged the proliferation of cesses and surcharges as distorting cooperative federalism.
• A key constitutional asymmetry: Parliament needs no Finance Commission consultation to impose surcharges, giving Union unilateral fiscal leverage.
• States' effective share is calculated on the divisible pool, not on gross tax revenue — the distinction matters enormously when cesses are large.

solution.concept_anchor: 15th Finance Commission horizontal distribution criteria and weights

statement_analysis.statement: Income Distance criterion carries the highest weight (45%) in the 15th Finance Commission's horizontal distribution formula.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th FC assigned 45% weight to Income Distance, making it the dominant equalisation parameter — States with lower per-capita income receive proportionally larger shares.

statement_analysis.statement: The 15th Finance Commission used 2001 census population data to avoid penalising States that had achieved better demographic performance.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th FC used 2011 census population data (15% weight), not 2001 data. A separate 'Demographic Performance' criterion (12.5%) was added to address southern States' concerns about being penalised for population control success.

statement_analysis.statement: Forest and Ecology carries a 10% weight in the 15th Finance Commission's horizontal distribution criteria.
statement_analysis.reason: Forest and Ecology was assigned exactly 10% weight by the 15th FC, recognizing that States maintaining large forest covers incur opportunity costs and provide environmental services.

statement_analysis.statement: Tax Effort and Area together account for 30% of the weight in the 15th Finance Commission's horizontal distribution formula.
statement_analysis.reason: Tax Effort carries 2.5% and Area carries 15%, summing to 17.5% — not 30%. Combining two real figures into a false total is a classic quantitative trap.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Selecting 'Only three' is tempting because students recall 2001 census being a contentious issue (used by 14th FC) and may mistakenly validate Statement 2, missing the 15th FC's shift to 2011 data.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Income Distance at 45% is the largest single weight in 15th FC formula — Correct.
Challenge Statement 2: 15th FC used 2011 census population, not 2001 — the 2001 figure was used by the 14th FC. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Forest and Ecology at 10% is correctly stated — Correct.
Challenge Statement 4: Tax Effort (2.5%) + Area (15%) = 17.5%, not 30% — Statement 4 is Incorrect. Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the well-known southern States' controversy about census data. Many students remember that 2001 census was demanded by southern States and that 14th FC used it, creating a false memory that 2011 data was avoided. In fact, the 15th FC used 2011 population data and separately introduced 'Demographic Performance' (12.5%) as a compensatory criterion — a nuanced distinction that separates thorough students from surface-level ones.
solution.final_explanation:
The 15th Finance Commission's horizontal distribution formula reflects a careful balance between equalisation (income distance), equity (forest/ecology), and efficiency incentives (demographic performance, tax effort).

Consider the following pairs regarding 15th Finance Commission horizontal criteria:

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Income Distance | 45% |
| Population (2011) | 15% |
| Area | 15% |
| Forest and Ecology | 10% |
| Demographic Performance | 12.5% |
| Tax Effort | 2.5% |

• Statement 1 — Correct: Income Distance at 45% is the largest weight, reflecting the equalisation mandate.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 2011 census data was used (not 2001). 'Demographic Performance' was added separately to compensate southern States.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Forest and Ecology at 10% is accurate.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Tax Effort (2.5%) + Area (15%) = 17.5%, not 30%.

Value Addition:
• Demographic Performance rewards States with lower fertility rates (below replacement level) — a direct response to southern States' objections.
• The 14th FC also used 2011 population data as well — the shift away from 1971 census happened at the 14th FC stage.
• Income Distance formula: each State's per-capita GSDP compared to the State with the highest per-capita GSDP — Haryana or Goa typically serve as the reference State.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional articles — grants and Finance Commission mandate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Pairing Article 282 with 'charged to Consolidated Fund' is the strongest trap because students know Article 275 grants come from CFI and conflate the two articles' appropriation mechanisms.
elimination_logic: Identify Article 280: President constitutes Finance Commission every 5 years — matches item 4 (quasi-judicial constitutional body constituted by President).
Identify Article 275: Statutory grants on Finance Commission recommendation, charged to Consolidated Fund — matches item 2 (grants charged to CFI, not subject to annual vote).
Identify Article 282: Discretionary grants for any public purpose, votable — matches item 3 (both Union and States may grant for public purpose, even outside legislative competence).
Identify Article 279: Defines 'net proceeds' with CAG certification — matches item 1. Correct combination is A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1 — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous conflation is between Articles 275 and 282. Both involve grants to/by States but differ fundamentally: Article 275 grants are Finance Commission-recommended, statutory, and charged to Consolidated Fund of India (not subject to vote). Article 282 grants are discretionary, votable, and can be made by both Union and States for any public purpose — even outside their legislative domain. Mixing their appropriation status (charged vs. voted) is the trap most candidates fall into.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 275, 280, 282, and 279 represent distinct pillars of the financial relations framework.

| List I (Article) | List II (Feature) |
|---|---|
| A. Article 279 | 1. Defines 'net proceeds'; CAG certifies the calculation |
| B. Article 275 | 2. Statutory grants to States charged to Consolidated Fund of India |
| C. Article 282 | 3. Both Union and States may make grants for any public purpose |
| D. Article 280 | 4. Quasi-judicial body constituted by President every five years |

Correct matching: A-4... wait — A is Article 279 (net proceeds/CAG) = 1; B is Article 275 (statutory grants/CFI) = 2; C is Article 282 (public purpose grants) = 3; D is Article 280 (Finance Commission) = 4.

• A-1: Article 279 defines net proceeds; CAG certifies — correct pairing.
• B-2: Article 275 grants are charged to CFI — not subject to annual Parliamentary vote.
• C-3: Article 282 is unique — both Union and States can grant, even beyond legislative competence.
• D-4: Article 280 establishes Finance Commission — constituted by President, functions quasi-judicially.

Value Addition:
• Article 275(1) has a proviso specifically for Scheduled Tribes welfare — a frequently tested detail.
• CSS are funded under Article 282 — allowing Union to direct spending in State subjects.
• Finance Commission recommendations on grants-in-aid (Art. 275) are binding in practice; Article 282 grants are discretionary.

solution.concept_anchor: GST Council voting — 3/4 majority and Union veto dynamics
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true instinctively select (a) without questioning whether the voting structure actually explains the Council's persuasive-only status — the causal link runs in the opposite direction from what (a) implies.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? The Supreme Court in Mohit Minerals (2022) held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding on Parliament or State legislatures — A is correct.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Under Article 279-A, Union holds 1/3 of votes and States collectively hold 2/3; decisions require 3/4 majority — R is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The persuasive nature of GST Council recommendations flows from the Constitution's silence on binding effect (confirmed by SC), not from the voting structure. The voting ratio is about internal decision-making, not the legal enforceability of outcomes. R does not explain A.

Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — select option (b)... Re-check: correct_option is (b). Confirm: option (b) states 'Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A' — matches.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know the Mohit Minerals judgment and the 3/4 voting rule will consider both A and R true and instinctively select (a) — the most common error in assertion-reason questions. The trap lies in the causal relationship: the persuasive nature of GST Council recommendations was established by the Supreme Court on the basis that Parliament and State legislatures retain their sovereign law-making power — not because of how votes are weighted internally. The voting structure governs whether a recommendation is made, not its legal force.
solution.final_explanation:
The GST Council under Article 279-A represents a constitutional innovation — a joint federal body for tax policy-making, inserted by the 101st Amendment.

Assertion (A): The Supreme Court in Mohit Minerals v. Union of India (2022) ruled that GST Council recommendations are not binding but merely persuasive. This is correct — the Court held that both Parliament and State legislatures retain their sovereign legislative authority and are not legally compelled to follow Council recommendations.

Reason (R): Article 279-A prescribes that Union holds 1/3 of votes and States collectively hold 2/3, with decisions requiring a 3/4 majority of votes cast. This is also factually correct — it means Union with ~33% votes cannot be outvoted unilaterally, giving it an effective veto.

Causal relationship: R describes the internal voting mechanism of the GST Council. The persuasive (non-binding) nature of recommendations is a constitutional interpretation question — established by the SC from the absence of any binding mandate in Article 279-A's text — not a consequence of vote distribution. The two facts are independent: recommendations could be non-binding regardless of vote shares.

Value Addition:
• The 3/4 majority rule means Union (1/3 votes) + any two large States can block a recommendation.
• GST Council has met over 50 times and operated largely by consensus — the binding vs. persuasive debate was mostly theoretical until Mohit Minerals.
• Article 279-A(9) provides that in case of dispute, Supreme Court has original jurisdiction — another rarely tested dimension.

solution.concept_anchor: Finance Commission devolution percentages — chronological evolution
solution.strong_distractor: c — Placing the 14th FC recommendation after the 15th FC's initial award seems implausible but candidates who misremember that 42% was a 15th FC figure will select this option.
elimination_logic: Anchor the sequence: 1st Finance Commission (~30%) is earliest — any option placing it later is wrong.
The 14th FC (2015–20) recommended 42% — a landmark jump. This must come before the 15th FC's main award.
The 15th FC gave two reports: 41% for 2020-21 (transition) and 41% for 2021-26 (main). These come after the 14th FC.
Correct sequence: 1st FC approximate share (1st) → 14th FC's 42% (2nd) → 15th FC transition year report (3rd) → 15th FC main report (4th). Option (b) reflects this — select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key confusion is between 42% (14th FC) and 41% (15th FC). Many students remember that the '42% was historic' and incorrectly assign it to the 15th FC. Additionally, the fact that the 15th FC issued two separate reports — one for the transition year 2020-21 and one for 2021-26 — is a rarely retained detail that creates additional chronological confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
Finance Commission vertical devolution recommendations have progressively evolved, with the 14th FC marking the most significant single-step increase.

Correct sequence:
1. 1st Finance Commission: Recommended approximately 30% of shareable taxes to States — the baseline era of limited devolution.
2. 14th Finance Commission (2015–20): Recommended 42% vertical devolution — a landmark 10-percentage-point jump, the largest in any single Finance Commission cycle.
3. 15th Finance Commission (First report, 2020-21 transition year): Recommended 41% devolution for the single transition year, marginally lower than 14th FC.
4. 15th Finance Commission (Main report, 2021-26): Maintained 41% for the full award period, with the reduction attributed to creation of J&K UTs and expanded centrally funded obligations.

Value Addition:
• The 42% figure applies to the divisible pool, not gross tax revenue of the Union — a critical distinction for calculating absolute transfer amounts.
• The 15th FC's reduction by 1 percentage point was accompanied by performance-linked grants to compensate States.
• Early Finance Commissions (1st–5th) operated in a centralised fiscal architecture; significant State-friendly shifts came post-Sarkaria Commission recommendations in the 1980s.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 282 — CSS funding mechanism and fiscal federalism tension
solution.strong_distractor: b — Article 275 sounds correct because it also involves Union-to-State financial transfers, and students may conflate Finance Commission–recommended statutory grants with the discretionary CSS mechanism.
elimination_logic: Identify what the scenario describes: Union directing spending in State subjects (Agriculture/Education) with matching fund conditions — this is the CSS mechanism.
Eliminate (a): Article 270 governs divisible pool distribution — it is an untied tax-sharing mechanism, not a grant-with-conditions mechanism.
Eliminate (b): Article 275 grants are Finance Commission-recommended, statutory, and charged to CFI — they are not the primary vehicle for Union directing State expenditure priorities.
Eliminate (c): Article 280 constitutes the Finance Commission — it is a body, not a funding mechanism. CSS are explicitly not within its framework.
Confirm (d): Article 282 allows Union to make grants for any public purpose — including in State subjects — and these are discretionary and votable, matching the scenario perfectly.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario tests whether students can distinguish four different financial transfer mechanisms. The key facts that point to Article 282: (1) Union directing spending in subjects on State List (Agriculture, Health, Education), (2) States required to contribute matching funds, (3) scheme design controlled by Union, and (4) Finance Commission framework bypassed. Only Article 282 permits this combination — but candidates conflate it with Article 275 (statutory FC-recommended grants) or mistakenly think Article 270 devolution covers it.
solution.final_explanation:
Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) are the primary instrument through which the Union government channels funds into State subjects, and their constitutional anchor is Article 282.

The scenario presents: Union funding agriculture extension in a State with conditionalities and matching fund requirements — bypassing Finance Commission — and States objecting to loss of autonomy. This precisely describes the CSS model.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 270 governs the divisible pool of shareable taxes. These are untied transfers — States face no conditions on how they spend devolved tax revenues. No matching funds required.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 275 grants are Finance Commission–recommended statutory grants, charged to the Consolidated Fund of India. They are not the mechanism for Union directing State agricultural spending with conditionalities.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission as a body. It is not itself a spending mechanism, and CSS explicitly bypass this framework — which is itself a source of criticism.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 282 permits the Union (and States) to make grants for public purposes even outside their legislative domain. This is the constitutional basis for CSS — giving Union discretion to fund State-subject schemes with conditions attached.

Value Addition:
• The 2015 rationalization reduced CSS from 66 to 28 umbrella schemes following recommendations to reduce Union overreach.
• 14th FC recommended reducing CSS and increasing tax devolution — recognizing the trade-off between tied grants and fiscal autonomy.
• States' matching contribution under CSS creates fiscal pressure, especially for smaller States with limited own revenue — a key federalism tension.

solution.concept_anchor: Expenditures charged to Consolidated Fund of India
solution.strong_distractor: c — Finance Commission grants (Article 275) being 'charged' to CFI is a less-known fact; students may think these are voted and thus select (c) as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify what 'charged to Consolidated Fund of India' means — these are non-votable expenditures that do not require annual Parliamentary approval.
Confirm: Salary of judges of Supreme Court — charged to CFI (Schedule II, Article 146(3)).
Confirm: Debt servicing (interest on loans) — charged to CFI (Article 292).
Confirm: Article 275 grants to States — charged to CFI, not subject to vote.

Test option (a): Contingency Fund advances — these come from the Contingency Fund (Article 267), which is a separate imprest account. Expenditure met from Contingency Fund is subsequently recouped from Consolidated Fund by Parliamentary appropriation. Contingency Fund advances are NOT directly 'charged' to CFI — select (a) as the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Contingency Fund trap: students know it exists alongside the Consolidated Fund and associate both with government finance. But 'charged to Consolidated Fund' has a specific constitutional meaning (non-votable expenditure), and Contingency Fund advances are an entirely different mechanism — an imprest account for urgent expenditure pending supplementary appropriation. Mixing the two funds is the core confusion this question exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
Expenditures 'charged to the Consolidated Fund of India' are non-votable — Parliament cannot reduce or reject them, though it can discuss them. They represent constitutionally guaranteed payments.

• Option (a) — Odd one out: Contingency Fund advances (Article 267) are drawn from a separate imprest account maintained for urgent unforeseen expenditure. These are not charged to the Consolidated Fund; they are later recouped through Parliamentary appropriation.
• Option (b) — Charged to CFI: Debt servicing (interest and principal on government loans) is explicitly charged to the Consolidated Fund under Article 292, making it non-votable.
• Option (c) — Charged to CFI: Article 275 grants recommended by the Finance Commission are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India — a less-known but examinable fact.
• Option (d) — Charged to CFI: Salaries of Supreme Court judges are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 146(3).

Value Addition:
• Other charged items include: President's salary, CAG's salary, Speaker/Deputy Speaker salaries, and sums required to satisfy court decrees.
• Contingency Fund is held at the disposal of the President (Article 267) — State-level equivalent is held by Governor.
• The distinction between 'voted' and 'charged' expenditure is a core concept in Parliamentary financial procedure.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 269 vs. Article 269-A — assigned vs. apportioned taxes

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 269, taxes on inter-State sale or purchase of goods (other than newspapers) were levied and collected by the Union, with the entire net proceeds assigned to the States — not shared with the Union.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 269 created a category of 'assigned' taxes where States received 100% of net proceeds. Post-GST, most transactions covered by Article 269 were subsumed into IGST under Article 269-A, but the original provision's mechanism remains correct as described.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 269-A, IGST on inter-State supplies is levied and collected by the Union, and the entire proceeds are assigned to the States in the same manner as Article 269 taxes.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 269-A creates a different mechanism: IGST proceeds are apportioned between the Union and States (not assigned 100% to States). Parliament prescribes the apportionment formula, unlike Article 269 where States receive the full net proceeds.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both statements sound similar because both describe Union levying and collecting taxes for inter-State transactions, making students think the outcome (State assignment) is the same in both cases.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 269 — levy and collection by Union, entire net proceeds assigned to States. This is accurate — States get 100%. Statement 1 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 269-A — IGST is apportioned between Union AND States, not assigned entirely to States. Statement 2 incorrectly equates 269-A with 269. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The proximity of Article 269 and Article 269-A in numbering, combined with the similarity of their subject matter (inter-State transactions), makes this one of the most exploited traps in fiscal federalism questions. The crucial difference: Article 269 = 100% to States (assigned); Article 269-A = shared between Union and States (apportioned). Candidates who know both articles exist but blur the distinction between 'assigned' and 'apportioned' will select (a) — the most common wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 269 and 269-A deal with inter-State transactions but with fundamentally different revenue-sharing outcomes.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 269 covered taxes on inter-State sale/purchase of goods, with net proceeds 100% assigned to States. The Union collected but retained nothing. Post-101st Amendment, most such transactions moved under IGST (Article 269-A) but the original Article 269 mechanism was as described.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 269-A created an apportionment model, not an assignment model. IGST revenue is shared between Union and States — the Union retains its share. This is a structurally different arrangement, and equating it with Article 269's 'assignment' is the central error.

Value Addition:
• 'Assigned' (Art. 269) = 100% to States; 'Apportioned' (Art. 269-A) = split between Union and States — the vocabulary distinction is constitutionally precise.
• Import transactions are also classified as inter-State supply under Article 269-A — a rare provision making IGST on imports shareable.
• The shift from Article 269's full-State assignment to Article 269-A's shared apportionment actually reduced States' gross inter-State tax receipts — partly why GST compensation was necessary.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 279 — net proceeds definition and CAG role
solution.strong_distractor: d — Attributing net proceeds certification to the Finance Commission feels logical because the Finance Commission decides how these proceeds are distributed, misleading students into conflating the computation authority with the distribution authority.
elimination_logic: Identify the blank: the constitutional authority that certifies 'net proceeds' of shareable taxes.
Eliminate (a): Controller General of Accounts handles government accounting but is not constitutionally empowered to certify net proceeds under Article 279.
Eliminate (c): RBI manages government banking but has no role in certifying tax net proceeds.
Eliminate (d): Finance Commission recommends distribution of net proceeds but does not certify their computation.
Confirm (b): Article 279 explicitly provides that the Comptroller and Auditor General certifies the net proceeds of taxes assigned to or shared with States — select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Finance Commission distractor (option d) is the primary trap: since the Finance Commission determines how net proceeds are divided, students assume it also certifies the computation. But Article 279 assigns certification to the CAG — an independent constitutional auditor — precisely to separate the audit function from the distribution recommendation function.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 279 of the Constitution defines 'net proceeds' as gross tax collection minus the cost of collection. The article also designates a specific constitutional authority to certify this computation.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Controller General of Accounts maintains Union government accounts but lacks the constitutional mandate under Article 279 to certify net proceeds.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is constituted under Article 148 and empowered under Article 279 to certify net proceeds — adding independent audit accountability to the tax-sharing framework.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Reserve Bank of India manages government banking and debt, but plays no role in certifying tax collection computations under Article 279.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Finance Commission recommends how net proceeds are to be divided but does not certify the computation — a separation of roles that is constitutionally significant.

Value Addition:
• CAG's certification is final for the purpose of Article 279 — it cannot be challenged except through constitutional channels.
• 'Net proceeds' matter because if collection costs are high, States' absolute share shrinks even if the percentage remains constant.
• CAG is appointed under Article 148 and serves as India's supreme audit institution — functions extend beyond net proceeds to auditing all public expenditure.

(d) Finance Commission of India

solution.concept_anchor: GST Compensation Cess — post-2022 extension purpose
solution.strong_distractor: b — Pairing the GST Compensation Cess with 'direct State compensation beyond June 2022' matches many students' general understanding of its purpose, missing the critical post-2022 shift in its application.
elimination_logic: Recall: GST Compensation Cess was originally levied on luxury/demerit goods to fund 14% guaranteed revenue growth for States for 5 years (till June 2022).
Post-June 2022: Cess was extended NOT to compensate States directly but to repay COVID-era back-to-back loans taken by Union on States' behalf.
Identify the correctly matched pair: the extended Cess (post-2022) is for loan repayment, not direct State compensation — option (d) states this correctly.
Options (a), (b), (c) either misstate the guarantee percentage, the duration, or the post-2022 purpose — (d) is the only correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The post-June 2022 purpose of the GST Compensation Cess is the trap. Most students know the Cess was extended beyond June 2022 but assume it continues to compensate States directly. The critical fact — that the extended Cess repays COVID-era back-to-back loans taken by the Union on States' behalf (not direct State revenue compensation) — distinguishes thorough preparation from surface knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 guaranteed States a 14% annual revenue growth rate for five years, with shortfalls funded by the GST Compensation Cess on luxury and demerit goods.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Compensation Cess was levied on luxury and demerit goods — not on all goods covered by GST. Extending the levy to all GST goods would describe a different policy entirely.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The original guarantee period ended in June 2022. The Cess was extended beyond June 2022, but its purpose shifted — it was no longer for direct State compensation but for repaying COVID-era loans.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The guaranteed revenue growth rate was 14% per annum, not 12%. This is a commonly tested quantitative trap.
• Option (d) — Correct: Post-June 2022, the GST Compensation Cess was extended specifically to repay the back-to-back loans that the Union government had borrowed on behalf of States during the COVID-19 period to cover compensation shortfalls — not for direct ongoing State compensation.

Value Addition:
• The 14% guaranteed growth was based on 2015-16 base year revenue — a reference point sometimes tested.
• Compensation Cess proceeds are kept in a separate Compensation Fund — outside the divisible pool.
• States' revenue autonomy concern post-GST: VAT, entry tax, octroi — all subsumed — leaving States dependent on GST devolution and centrally decided IGST apportionment.

solution.concept_anchor: Divisible pool composition — post-101st Amendment

statement_analysis.statement: After the 101st Constitutional Amendment, CGST (Central GST) collected by the Union forms part of the divisible pool under Article 270 and is shared with States through Finance Commission–recommended percentages.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-101st Amendment, Article 270 was amended to include CGST and additional excise duties on goods covered under GST within the divisible pool — subjecting them to Finance Commission–determined devolution.

statement_analysis.statement: Surcharges levied by Parliament under Article 271 on any Union List tax are included in the divisible pool to the extent of 50% of their proceeds.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 271 explicitly excludes surcharges entirely from the divisible pool — States receive zero share. There is no 50% or any partial sharing of surcharge proceeds.

statement_analysis.statement: IGST proceeds collected on inter-State supplies are NOT part of the divisible pool under Article 270 — they are apportioned separately under Article 269-A.
statement_analysis.reason: IGST operates under a distinct apportionment mechanism under Article 269-A, explicitly separate from the divisible pool. Finance Commission has no role in IGST distribution.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three appears correct because Statements 1 and 3 are accurate and the surcharge provision (Statement 2) is often misremembered as involving partial sharing.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Post-101st Amendment, CGST is within Article 270 divisible pool — Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 271 surcharges go 100% to Union — no 50% sharing provision exists. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: IGST is outside divisible pool, governed by Article 269-A — Correct.
Correct statements are 1 and 3 only — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the targeted trap: the phrase '50% of their proceeds' sounds like a reasonable constitutional compromise and tempts students who remember surcharges are somehow restricted but cannot recall the exact rule. In reality, surcharges are wholly Union revenue under Article 271 — the 50% figure is a complete fabrication designed to test precision.
solution.final_explanation:
The divisible pool under Article 270 is the central mechanism of Union-State fiscal federalism, and its composition has evolved with constitutional amendments.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 101st Amendment restructured Article 270 to bring CGST into the divisible pool. Finance Commission–recommended percentages now govern how CGST is split between Union and States.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 271 provides no partial sharing of surcharges. The entire proceeds of surcharges go to the Union — States receive nothing. The '50% sharing' concept has no constitutional basis.
• Statement 3 — Correct: IGST sits outside Article 270's divisible pool. It is governed by Article 269-A's separate apportionment framework — Parliament legislates the formula on GST Council's recommendation. Finance Commission plays no role.

Value Addition:
• The divisible pool formula: All Union taxes EXCEPT those under Articles 268, 269, 269-A, surcharges (Art. 271), and cesses form the pool.
• Post-GST, the divisible pool's composition changed significantly — traditional excise and service tax replaced by CGST within the pool.
• States' share from divisible pool: 41% (15th FC) — but effective receipts depend on actual tax collections, not just percentages.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 275(1) proviso — Scheduled Tribes welfare grants
solution.strong_distractor: c — Stating that Article 275 grants are subject to annual Parliamentary vote sounds procedurally reasonable, but these grants are specifically charged to the Consolidated Fund — making them non-votable.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Article 275 grants are not discretionary — they are Finance Commission–recommended statutory grants. Discretionary grants flow from Article 282.
Eliminate (c): Article 275 grants are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India — they are not subject to annual Parliamentary vote, distinguishing them from Article 282 grants.
Eliminate (d): Article 275 does not restrict grants to North-Eastern States alone — any State in need may receive grants; and the Scheduled Tribes proviso applies broadly.

Confirm (b): Article 275(1) contains a specific proviso for grants to States for promoting welfare of Scheduled Tribes and raising the level of administration of Scheduled Areas — this is the correct and specific description.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth in option (c) — suggesting Article 275 grants are voted — exploits a common confusion between Articles 275 and 282. Since Article 282 grants ARE voted (and are the more commonly discussed vehicle for Centre-State transfers), students apply Article 282's appropriation logic to Article 275, getting the answer wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 275 provides for statutory grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India to States in need, on the recommendation of the Finance Commission.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 275 grants are not discretionary. They flow from Finance Commission recommendations — making them statutory. Discretionary grants (Union's choice, no FC recommendation needed) are governed by Article 282.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 275(1) contains a specific proviso that Parliament shall provide grants for two purposes: (i) promoting welfare of Scheduled Tribes in a State, and (ii) raising the level of administration of Scheduled Areas, to the standard prevailing in the rest of the State.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 275 grants are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India — they are non-votable. This is a key distinction from Article 282 grants, which are voted.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 275 is not restricted to North-Eastern States. Any State that needs assistance qualifies, and the Scheduled Tribes proviso applies nationally.

Value Addition:
• The Scheduled Tribes proviso in Article 275(1) is among the earliest affirmative fiscal provisions for tribal welfare in the Constitution.
• Finance Commission can recommend differential grants — different amounts to different States based on assessed need.
• 15th FC recommended sector-specific grants (health, education, local bodies, disaster risk) under Article 275 framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 286 restriction and Article 304 non-discrimination principle

statement_analysis.statement: Article 286 of the Constitution prohibits States from levying any tax on goods imported from or exported to another country, thereby protecting international trade from State-level taxation.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 286 prohibits States from taxing inter-State sales and purchases of goods — it concerns inter-State trade within India, not international trade. Taxes on imports from foreign countries fall under Union's domain (customs), not Article 286.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 304 allows a State to impose a tax on goods imported from other States or Union territories if and only if similar goods manufactured or produced within the State are subject to an equivalent tax — thus preventing discriminatory taxation.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 304(a) permits non-discriminatory State taxation on imported goods — a State can tax goods from other States only at a rate not exceeding the tax on similar locally produced goods, ensuring equal treatment.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2016) struck down all State entry taxes as unconstitutional since entry taxes violate the freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse guaranteed under Article 301.
statement_analysis.reason: The SC in Jindal Stainless (2016) upheld entry taxes as constitutionally valid — it rejected the 'compensatory theory' test as the sole basis for validity. Entry taxes were not struck down; they were accepted as a legitimate State fiscal tool subject to non-discrimination, and were subsequently subsumed under GST.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three as incorrect tempts students who know Articles 286 and 304 but misremember the Jindal Stainless judgment outcome — many recall the case involved entry taxes and 'struck down' sounds plausible.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Article 286 restricts inter-State trade taxation, not international trade. Describing it as protecting 'international trade' is factually wrong. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Test Statement 2: Article 304(a) precisely describes non-discriminatory equivalent taxation on goods from other States — this is accurate. Statement 2 is Correct.
Test Statement 3: Jindal Stainless (2016) upheld State entry taxes — it did NOT strike them down. Stating the SC 'struck down all entry taxes' is factually wrong. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Statements NOT correct: 1 and 3 — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Jindal Stainless trap is especially effective: students who know the case dealt with entry taxes and the Article 301 freedom of trade often confuse the outcome. The Court rejected the old 'compensatory theory' (which had been used to justify entry taxes as fees for services) but upheld entry taxes on a broader basis — non-discriminatory taxes on commerce are valid even without compensatory justification. The case is frequently cited as 'struck down entry taxes' by candidates who confuse the legal reasoning with the outcome.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 286 and 304 form the constitutional framework preventing States from creating inter-State trade barriers through discriminatory taxation.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 286 restricts State-level taxation of inter-State sale and purchase of goods within India — not international trade. Import duties on foreign goods fall under Entry 83 of the Union List (customs).
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 304(a) precisely permits States to tax goods from other States at rates equal to (not higher than) the tax on similar locally produced goods — a non-discrimination principle preserving the unity of India's common market.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Jindal Stainless (nine-judge Constitutional Bench, 2016) upheld entry taxes as constitutionally valid. It overruled the compensatory theory test but did not invalidate entry taxes. These were subsequently subsumed under GST in 2017.

Value Addition:
• Article 301 guarantees freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout India — but Article 304 allows States to deviate for non-discriminatory taxes and reasonable restrictions in public interest.
• Pre-GST, octroi and entry tax were major State revenue sources — their subsuming under GST is a key cause of States' revenue loss concerns.
• Article 302 empowers Parliament to impose restrictions on inter-State trade in public interest — Union has wider powers than States under this framework.

solution.concept_anchor: 15th Finance Commission — two reports and devolution ratios

statement_analysis.statement: The 15th Finance Commission submitted two separate reports — one for the transition year 2020-21 and a main report for 2021-26 — with different recommendations in each.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th FC submitted its first report for 2020-21 (transition year, due to the pandemic and constitutional timeline) and its main report covering 2021-26 — both with distinct devolution and grant recommendations.

statement_analysis.statement: The 15th Finance Commission recommended 42% vertical devolution from the divisible pool to States for the period 2021-26.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th FC recommended 41% (not 42%) for both 2020-21 and 2021-26. The 42% figure was the 14th Finance Commission's landmark recommendation.

statement_analysis.statement: The 15th Finance Commission introduced performance-based grants for States linked to outcomes in health, education, and local body governance.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th FC introduced sector-specific performance-linked grants — a new approach conditioning additional grants on measurable outcomes in health, education, agriculture, and urban/rural local body performance.

statement_analysis.statement: The marginal reduction in vertical devolution by the 15th Finance Commission (compared to the 14th Finance Commission) was partly attributed to the creation of new Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
statement_analysis.reason: The 15th FC cited the reorganization of J&K into two UTs (reducing the divisible pool's State-claimant base and increasing Union's direct responsibility for these territories) as a reason for the 1-percentage-point reduction from 42% to 41%.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Selecting 'Only three' is tempting because most students know statements 1, 3, and 4 are accurate but may accept Statement 2's 42% figure as correct, having confused 14th and 15th FC recommendations.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Two reports — 2020-21 transition and 2021-26 main — confirmed. Correct.
Challenge Statement 2: 42% was the 14th FC. 15th FC recommended 41%. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Performance-linked grants introduced by 15th FC — confirmed. Correct.
Confirm Statement 4: J&K UT creation cited as reason for reduction — confirmed by 15th FC report. Correct.
Three correct statements (1, 3, 4) — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 42% vs. 41% trap is one of the most reliably tested numerical confusions in Finance Commission questions. Students who remember '14th FC made a landmark jump to 42%' sometimes attribute this to the 15th FC as well, especially under time pressure. Statement 2 is constructed to exploit this — it contains an authoritative-sounding context but substitutes the wrong percentage.
solution.final_explanation:
The 15th Finance Commission's recommendations represent both continuity and innovation in India's fiscal federalism architecture.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Statement 1 (Two reports) | Correct |
| Statement 2 (42% devolution) | Incorrect — 15th FC recommended 41% |
| Statement 3 (Performance grants) | Correct |
| Statement 4 (J&K UT linkage) | Correct |

• Statement 2 is the only incorrect statement. The 14th FC recommended 42%; the 15th FC marginally reduced this to 41%, and multiple factors were cited — J&K reorganization and increased centrally funded obligations being primary.
• Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct.

Value Addition:
• The 15th FC's performance-linked grants were a structural shift from input-based to outcome-based fiscal transfers.
• The 15th FC also recommended a National Disaster Risk Management Fund and State Disaster Risk Management Funds — fiscal federalism in disaster financing.
• Both 15th FC reports must be studied separately — devolution ratio was the same (41%) in both, but grant recommendations differed significantly between the transition year and main award.

concepts_used: Tax Devolution vs. Grants: Untied vs. Tied Funds Debate
Article 282: Discretionary Grants — Union and State Contributions for Public Purpose

solution.concept_anchor: 14th FC policy shift — raised devolution, reduced grants
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know both A and R as true facts may doubt whether the Finance Commission's policy choice truly 'explains' the untied nature of devolved taxes, questioning if R is just a consequence rather than a cause.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? The 14th Finance Commission consciously raised vertical devolution to 42% and simultaneously recommended reducing centrally sponsored schemes — aimed at expanding States' untied fiscal space. A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Tax devolution under Articles 269/270 carries no conditions — States spend these funds as per their own priorities, unlike grants under Article 282 which come with Union-set conditionalities. R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes. The 14th FC's rationale for raising devolution and reducing grants was precisely that devolved taxes are untied (the fact stated in R) — giving States greater fiscal autonomy than conditional grants. R directly explains the policy logic behind A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A — select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The 14th Finance Commission's decision to recommend 42% devolution (from 32% under the 13th FC) was a deliberate policy choice grounded in the distinction between untied devolution and tied grants.

Assertion (A): The 14th FC recommended raising vertical devolution and reducing CSS (Centrally Sponsored Schemes) — this is historically accurate. The Commission explicitly stated this was intended to enhance States' fiscal autonomy by increasing resources they control without Union conditionalities.

Reason (R): Tax devolution under Articles 270 and 269 is constitutionally untied — States spend devolved funds without any Union-mandated conditions. This is accurate: once funds enter State Consolidated Funds via devolution, States decide spending priorities.

Causal relationship: R is the direct rationale for the 14th FC's policy documented in A. The Commission reasoned: since devolved taxes give States genuine autonomy (R), increasing devolution (A) is the superior instrument for strengthening cooperative federalism compared to grants with conditions.

Value Addition:
• The trade-off: higher devolution means States bear all spending risk; grants allow Union to direct investment in national priority sectors.
• 14th FC's approach was praised by State governments and criticized by Union ministries that lost CSS funding influence.
• NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission in 2015 — partly as a response to the changing CSS/devolution balance recommended by 14th FC.

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 268–271 — levy, collection, and appropriation mechanisms
solution.strong_distractor: b — Swapping Article 268 (collected by States) with Article 269 (assigned to States) is the most common error; both result in States receiving 100% but via different constitutional mechanisms, making the swap feel correct.
elimination_logic: Article 268: Union levies, States collect AND appropriate (keep 100%). Matches item 3 (States collect and retain entire proceeds — not shareable).
Article 269: Union levies and collects; entire net proceeds 'assigned' to States (100% to States). Matches item 1 (net proceeds assigned entirely to States; Finance Commission has no role).

Article 270: Union levies and collects; proceeds shared between Union and States through Finance Commission. Matches item 4 (divisible pool; Finance Commission determines vertical and horizontal distribution).
Article 271: Parliament imposes surcharge; entire proceeds go to Union — no State share. Matches item 2. Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Articles 268 and 269 create an almost identical outcome for States (100% of proceeds) but through mechanically different constitutional routes: under 268, States collect and appropriate; under 269, Union collects and assigns. The options are designed so that swapping these two (matching 268 with item 1 and 269 with item 3) produces a plausible-looking but wrong answer — conflating 'collected by States' with 'assigned to States'.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 268–271 constitute the core architecture of tax distribution, each with a distinct mechanism.

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Article 268 | 1. Taxes levied and collected by Union; net proceeds wholly assigned to States; Finance Commission has no role in distribution |
| B. Article 269 | 2. Parliament may levy surcharge on Union List taxes; proceeds go entirely to the Union — States receive no share |
| C. Article 270 | 3. Taxes levied by Union; States collect and retain entire proceeds within their territory — Union receives nothing |
| D. Article 271 | 4. Taxes levied and collected by Union; proceeds shared between Union and States; Finance Commission determines distribution ratios |

Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2

• A (268)-3: Stamp duties — Union levies, States collect and appropriate 100%.
• B (269)-1: Inter-State goods taxes — Union levies and collects, 100% assigned to States.
• C (270)-4: Core divisible pool — Finance Commission determines vertical (Union-State) and horizontal (among States) distribution.
• D (271)-2: Surcharges — 100% to Union, entirely excluded from divisible pool.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between Art. 268 ('collected by States') and Art. 269 ('assigned to States') is constitutional vocabulary — not merely stylistic difference.
• Post-GST, Art. 269 coverage has narrowed significantly (newspapers remain the main residual item).
• Art. 270 is the most fiscally significant article — covering income tax, corporation tax, and CGST post-101st Amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: GST Council — 3/4 majority requirement and Union's effective veto
solution.strong_distractor: a — Concluding that a 2/3 majority suffices because States hold 2/3 of votes feels mathematically intuitive but misapplies the voting threshold, which requires 3/4 of total votes cast.
elimination_logic: Identify the constitutional rule: Article 279-A requires decisions by 3/4 majority of votes cast — Union has 1/3 votes, States have 2/3.

Calculate: 3/4 majority threshold means any decision requires support from votes totaling 75% of votes cast. Union's 1/3 (≈33%) means if Union votes against, States need all their 2/3 votes PLUS some additional votes they don't have — Union can effectively block any resolution.
Eliminate (a): A simple 2/3 majority of States alone would be 2/3 of 2/3 = 4/9 of total votes — well below the 3/4 threshold. States cannot pass a resolution without some Union support.
Eliminate (b): A simple majority (51%) would be below the 3/4 constitutional requirement — not the correct threshold.
Eliminate (d): Unanimous consent is not required by Article 279-A — 3/4 suffices, not 100%.
Confirm (c): Union can effectively veto because a 3/4 majority requires Union's support — if Union votes against, the mathematical threshold cannot be met by States alone.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap: students know States have 2/3 votes and may conclude States can pass resolutions independently (since 2/3 > 1/2). But the 3/4 threshold means Union's 1/3 share is effectively a blocking minority — without Union support, States' 2/3 votes fall short of 3/4. This mathematical precision is what distinguishes correct constitutional understanding from superficial recall.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 279-A(6) prescribes that every decision of the GST Council shall be taken at a meeting by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting.

The scenario presents: States with 24 out of 32 total votes (= 3/4 exactly) try to pass a resolution on GST rate rationalization with Union voting against.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: States holding 2/3 of votes cannot pass a resolution independently. If Union (1/3 votes) votes against, States have only 2/3 of total votes — below the 3/4 threshold. A 2/3 State majority is insufficient.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Simple majority (>50%) is not the constitutional standard. The 3/4 weighted majority requirement is explicit under Article 279-A(6).
• Option (c) — Correct: Since States hold exactly 2/3 of votes and the threshold is 3/4, States voting unanimously (2/3 = ~67%) still fall below 75%. They need at least some Union support to reach 3/4. Union effectively has a veto — the resolution fails.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Unanimity is not required. A 3/4 majority suffices for decisions — but even this cannot be achieved without Union's votes.

Value Addition:
• In practice, GST Council decisions have been taken by consensus in most meetings — the voting rule is a constitutional backstop, rarely invoked.
• The Mohit Minerals (2022) SC judgment confirmed that even decisions taken under Article 279-A remain recommendations — not binding laws.
• The 1/3:2/3 vote split reflects federal balance: Union alone cannot decide (needs support), but States alone also cannot decide (need Union's share or near-unanimous State support).

solution.concept_anchor: Finance Commission — constitutional body vs. extra-constitutional distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — GST Council being a constitutional body (inserted by 101st Amendment) may lead students to group it with Finance Commission as the 'odd extra-constitutional body,' overlooking that NITI Aayog is the actual extra-constitutional entity.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: constitutional bodies established through specific constitutional provisions.
Finance Commission (Art. 280) — constitutional body. Belongs.
GST Council (Art. 279-A, 101st Amendment) — constitutional body. Belongs.
Comptroller and Auditor General (Art. 148) — constitutional body. Belongs.
NITI Aayog — established by Cabinet resolution in January 2015, with NO constitutional basis. It is extra-constitutional — the odd one out. Select (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission, and students may associate 'Planning Commission' (extra-constitutional) correctly but forget that NITI Aayog — its successor — is equally extra-constitutional, established only by executive order. Meanwhile, the GST Council's constitutional status (Article 279-A) may be forgotten, causing students to misidentify it as extra-constitutional instead.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the ability to distinguish constitutional bodies from those established by executive action.

• Option (a) — Finance Commission: Established under Article 280 — a clearly constitutional body, constituted by the President every five years. Belongs to the group.
• Option (b) — GST Council: Established under Article 279-A, inserted by the 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016). It is a constitutional body — belongs to the group.
• Option (c) — Comptroller and Auditor General: Established under Article 148 of the Constitution — one of the oldest constitutional authorities. Belongs to the group.
• Option (d) — NITI Aayog: Established by a Cabinet resolution on January 1, 2015 — no constitutional provision mandates or creates it. It is an executive/extra-constitutional body. This is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• NITI Aayog's predecessor, Planning Commission, was also extra-constitutional — established by executive resolution in 1950.
• Finance Commission is described as quasi-judicial because it examines evidence, hears representations, and gives reasoned recommendations — not merely advisory.
• GST Council's constitutional status makes it the first federal body with joint tax policy-making power — a structural departure from India's earlier fiscal architecture.

solution.concept_anchor: IGST — outside Finance Commission framework; divisible pool percentage applies only to pool

statement_analysis.statement: IGST revenue from inter-State supplies is NOT part of the Finance Commission's divisible pool — its distribution between the Union and States is determined through a separate mechanism under Article 269-A.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 269-A creates an independent apportionment mechanism for IGST, with Parliament prescribing the formula on GST Council's recommendation. Finance Commission has no mandate over IGST distribution.

statement_analysis.statement: When the 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% devolution to States, this 41% figure applies to the Union's gross tax revenue including IGST, corporation tax, income tax, and all cess and surcharge collections.
statement_analysis.reason: The 41% applies only to the divisible pool — which excludes IGST (governed by Art. 269-A), surcharges (Art. 271), cesses, and taxes under Art. 268 and 269. Applying 41% to gross tax revenue significantly overstates States' receipts.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both statements appear plausible to a student who knows IGST is outside the Finance Commission framework (confirming Statement 1) but hasn't precisely defined what 'divisible pool' means (accepting Statement 2's overstatement).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: IGST distribution is under Article 269-A, separate from Finance Commission — confirmed. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The 41% figure applies to the divisible pool, not gross tax revenue. Gross tax revenue includes IGST, cesses, and surcharges — all of which are outside the divisible pool. Statement 2 overstates the base and is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'gross tax revenue vs. divisible pool' confusion is perhaps the most consequential numerical trap in Finance Commission questions. When students see '41% to States' and apply it to total Union taxes, they dramatically overestimate fiscal transfers. The divisible pool is a subset of gross tax revenue — IGST, surcharges, and cesses are all excluded. Statement 2 is crafted to exploit this by listing specific taxes (including IGST and cesses) that should NOT be in the base.
solution.final_explanation:
The precision of fiscal federalism language — especially 'divisible pool' vs. 'gross tax revenue' — determines whether numerical devolution claims are accurate.

• Statement 1 — Correct: IGST has its own constitutional distribution framework under Article 269-A. Finance Commission's mandate under Article 280 covers only the divisible pool — it cannot recommend how IGST is split. This is a major structural feature of post-GST fiscal architecture.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The divisible pool is explicitly defined by exclusions. It does NOT include: (i) IGST (Art. 269-A), (ii) taxes assigned under Art. 269, (iii) taxes collected by States under Art. 268, (iv) surcharges (Art. 271), (v) cesses. The 41% applies to this narrower base — not to gross tax revenue that includes all these items.

Value Addition:
• The practical gap: Union's gross tax revenue may be ₹30 lakh crore, but divisible pool may be only ₹18–20 lakh crore after exclusions. States receive 41% of the latter.
• This structural gap — especially the growing share of cesses/surcharges outside the pool — is the central fiscal federalism grievance of States.
• Finance Commission reports explicitly compute the divisible pool projections — an important number to track in budget documents.

Article 268-A (Repealed): Service Tax — Historical and Post-GST Significance

solution.concept_anchor: 88th Amendment — Article 268-A insertion for service tax
solution.strong_distractor: c — The 92nd Amendment sounds plausible as a mid-2000s constitutional amendment, and candidates who approximate the amendment number without precise recall will select it.
elimination_logic: Identify the constitutional event: Service tax sharing framework via a new article was operationalized in 2003 by an amendment.
Eliminate (b): The 80th Amendment (2000) dealt with the alternate formula for tax devolution following the Tenth Finance Commission — unrelated to service tax.
Eliminate (c): The 92nd Amendment (2003) dealt with inclusion of Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali in the Eighth Schedule — unrelated to service tax.
Eliminate (d): The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST and repealed Article 268-A — it did not insert it.
Confirm (a): The 88th Constitutional Amendment (2003) inserted Article 268-A to constitutionalize service tax sharing between Union and States — select (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 88th vs. 101st Amendment confusion is the primary trap: students know the 101st Amendment is GST-related and that it repealed Article 268-A. Under time pressure, they may confuse 'inserted' with 'repealed' and select the 101st Amendment. The 92nd Amendment distractor (same year, 2003) adds temporal confusion for candidates who remember '2003 constitutional amendment' without pinning down the specific number.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 268-A had a brief but constitutionally significant existence — inserted to give service tax a constitutional home and later repealed when GST absorbed service tax.

• Option (a) — Correct: The 88th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 inserted Article 268-A into the Constitution, providing a constitutional framework for Parliament to levy taxes on services and for the proceeds to be distributed between Union and States.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 80th Amendment (2000) related to the alternate formula for sharing proceeds of income tax and excise duties following the Tenth Finance Commission's recommendations — entirely different subject matter.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 92nd Amendment (2003) added four languages (Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali) to the Eighth Schedule — no connection to service tax.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST and simultaneously repealed Article 268-A — it ended, not began, Article 268-A's existence.

Value Addition:
• Article 268-A was inserted but was never made fully operational before GST came into force — service tax continued under Finance Acts.
• The 88th Amendment also amended Article 270 to include service tax within the divisible pool framework.
• Constitutional evolution lesson: Articles can be inserted and repealed within 13 years — reflecting dynamic federal fiscal negotiations.

solution.concept_anchor: CSS rationalization 2015 — from 66 to 28 umbrella schemes

statement_analysis.statement: In 2015, the Union government rationalized Centrally Sponsored Schemes by consolidating them from 66 schemes into 28 umbrella schemes, partly in response to recommendations for expanding States' discretionary fiscal space.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2015 rationalization exercise reduced CSS from 66 to 28 umbrella schemes, implemented alongside the 14th FC's recommendation to reduce tied grants and increase devolution — both aimed at enhancing State fiscal autonomy.

statement_analysis.statement: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are financed under Article 275 of the Constitution, which specifically empowers the Union to direct spending in State-subject areas for national priority purposes.
statement_analysis.reason: CSS are funded under Article 282, not Article 275. Article 275 provides Finance Commission-recommended statutory grants; Article 282 provides discretionary grants for any public purpose — the constitutional basis for CSS.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Centrally Sponsored Schemes, States are often required to contribute a matching share from their own budgets, which critics argue creates fiscal pressure particularly for revenue-deficit States.
statement_analysis.reason: CSS matching fund requirements — where States must contribute 30-40% of scheme costs — create genuine fiscal pressure, particularly for smaller or revenue-deficit States that must divert funds from their own priorities to avail Union funds.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting all three statements as correct is tempting because Statement 2's error (Article 275 vs. 282) is subtle — both are grant-giving articles and candidates who know CSS involves grants may not recall which specific article applies.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: 2015 rationalization — 66 to 28 umbrella CSS — confirmed as historically accurate. Statement 1 is Correct.
Challenge Statement 2: CSS are funded under Article 282 (discretionary grants), not Article 275 (FC-recommended statutory grants). The article attribution is wrong. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: State matching fund requirements in CSS — a well-established fiscal federalism concern. Statement 3 is Correct.
Correct statements: 1 and 3 only — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits Article 275 vs. 282 conflation — both involve Union grants, but Article 275 is Finance Commission-recommended and statutory, while Article 282 is discretionary and the actual CSS vehicle. The difference matters constitutionally: if CSS were under Article 275, States would have Finance Commission protection; under Article 282, Union exercises unilateral discretion. Candidates who recall 'CSS involve grants' without pinning the article number will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Centrally Sponsored Schemes sit at the intersection of cooperative federalism and fiscal dependence — their constitutional basis and fiscal mechanics are both examinable.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 2015 rationalization reduced CSS from 66 to 28 umbrella schemes. This was a response to the 14th FC's recommendation to reduce tied grants and increase tax devolution — recognizing that conditioned grants constrain State fiscal autonomy.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CSS are financed under Article 282, not Article 275. Article 282 permits Union (and States) to make discretionary grants for public purposes — even in subjects within the other level's legislative domain. Article 275 grants require Finance Commission recommendation and are charged to CFI.
• Statement 3 — Correct: State matching contributions (typically 30-40% for general States, lower for special category States) under CSS create real fiscal pressure — States must commit own resources to Union-designed programmes, limiting their spending autonomy.

Value Addition:
• Despite rationalization, States continue to argue that conditionalities remain even within umbrella CSS — 'rationalization' reduced numbers, not necessarily Union control.
• Special Category States (hill, tribal, island States) face lower matching contribution requirements — a built-in equity mechanism.
• 15th FC recommended State governments be given more flexibility in CSS implementation — reflecting ongoing federalism tension.
